title: Choose the structure

outcomes.can: Pick a data structure by the operation a problem repeats most often.
Recognize when sorting first makes a problem a single pass.
Model a new problem as a graph and choose the search that fits.

intro: This last module has no new structures. Real problems do not say which structure to use, so the skill that remains is choosing. The module gives a short way to decide, shows how much the choice can matter, and then sets three problems with no hint about which earlier module they belong to.

steps.title: Ask what is repeated
steps.text:
To choose a structure, find the operation the solution performs again and again, and pick the structure that makes that one operation cheap.

| The repeated operation | Structure | Cost of it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read by position | Array | O(1) |
| Is this value present? Look up by key | Set or Map | O(1) on average |
| Take the most recent | Stack | O(1) |
| Take the oldest | Queue | O(1) |
| Take the smallest | Heap | O(log n) |
| Find a position in ordered data | Sorted array with binary search | O(log n) |
| Insert or remove next to a known place | Linked list | O(1) |

Then ask the same of the algorithm. Does the problem have the shape of a walk through connected things, of a choice built from smaller choices, or of a single pass that only needs the data in order?

steps.title: Predict the difference
steps.text: Both halves of the example answer one question: does any number in a also appear in b? Predict the two step counts.

steps.title: Sort first
steps.text:
A second move is worth as much as the first: **put the data in order before working on it**. Sorting costs O(n log n), and it often turns the rest of the problem into one pass.

- After sorting, equal items are next to each other, so duplicates and groups are found by comparing neighbours.
- After sorting by start time, things that overlap are next to each other.
- After sorting, binary search and two pointers both become available.

When a problem seems to need every pair compared, ask whether an order exists in which only neighbours matter.

steps.title: Predict a sweep
steps.text: The example sorts meetings by start time and then compares each with the one before it. Predict both lines.

steps.title: Merge overlapping ranges
steps.text: Work from the prompt. Decide what order would make this a single pass.

steps.title: Group words by their letters
steps.text: Work from the prompt. Decide what two words in the same group have in common, and how to look that up.

steps.title: Find the shortest way through a grid
steps.text: Work from the prompt. Decide what the nodes and the connections are.

choices.feedback: The nested loops run the inner loop a thousand times for each of a thousand numbers.

The nested loops compare every pair: a million steps. The Set version spends 1,000 steps building a Set from `b` and 1,000 lookups. The repeated question was "is this value in b?", and a Set answers it in one step where an array needs a scan. Most speed-ups in everyday code are this one.
A lookup in a Set is one step, however many values it holds.

questions.prompt: What does the second line print?

choices.feedback: After sorting, the meetings read 9 to 10, 9 to 11, 13 to 15 and 14 to 16. 9 to 11 starts before 9 to 10 ends, and 14 to 16 starts before 13 to 15 ends. Sorted, three neighbour comparisons were enough, where unsorted data would need every meeting compared with every other. The first exercise extends this to merging the overlapping ranges.
There are two overlapping pairs: the two morning meetings, and the two afternoon ones.
Only neighbours in the sorted list are compared, and two of those three comparisons find an overlap.

review.evidence: Open a fresh starter on a later visit, with the earlier answer closed. A first unaided pass on every case is later evidence of the skill. A hinted pass stays recorded as assisted.
